title: Connected smooth normal subgroups of reductive groups are reductive
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $G$ be a reductive affine $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], where reductivity has the meaning of [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]: $G$ is smooth and connected and has no nontrivial smooth connected closed normal unipotent subgroup. Here smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme], and unipotent means that in a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation every geometric point $u$ satisfies $(u-I)^n=0$ for some $n\geq1$. Let $M\subseteq G$ be a smooth connected closed normal subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Then $M$ is reductive. The trivial subgroup is included; no characteristic-zero or semisimplicity hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Corollary 21.53, printed p.441: every connected normal subgroup variety of a reductive group is reductive. Group variety means smooth algebraic group; smoothness of M is retained explicitly.

proof.text: Write $G=\operatorname{Spec}A$. By [lem-weil-pbc-lft-affine-pairs], $A$ is a finitely generated $F$-algebra. The closed immersion $M\hookrightarrow G$ gives $M=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$ by [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Images of generators of $A$ generate $A/I$, so $M$ is affine of finite type by [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. It is smooth and connected by hypothesis. Apply [lem-sfb-unipotent-radical-existence] to $M$, obtaining its largest smooth connected closed normal unipotent subgroup $U$. The composite $U\hookrightarrow M\hookrightarrow G$ is a closed immersion: its coordinate map is a composite of surjections. Hence $U$ is also affine of finite type as a closed subgroup of $G$.

source.place: Section 6.46, p.135; affine closed-subscheme description: Stacks Tag 01QO, morphisms.tex lemma-characterize-closed-immersion.

proof.text: Fix $g\in G(F)$. Normality of $M$ in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] makes $c_g:m\mapsto gmg^{-1}$ an $F$-group-scheme automorphism of $M$, with inverse $c_{g^{-1}}$. Its image subgroup $V=c_g(U)$ is isomorphic to $U$; it is closed, smooth and connected by the definitions [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. For every $F$-algebra $B$, normality follows from $m c_g(u)m^{-1}=c_g(c_g^{-1}(m)u c_g^{-1}(m)^{-1})$ for $m\in M(B)$ and $u\in U(B)$. If $r$ is a faithful unipotent representation of $U$, then $r\circ(c_g|_U)^{-1}$ is one of $V$, with the identical matrices over every algebraically closed extension field [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure]. The largest-subgroup assertion of [lem-sfb-unipotent-radical-existence] gives $c_g(U)\subseteq U$ as subgroup schemes. Apply the same assertion to $g^{-1}$ and conjugate back to get $U\subseteq c_g(U)$. Thus $c_g(U)=U$ as closed subgroup schemes of $G$.

source.place: Section 6.46, p.135: largest-subgroup uniqueness; Corollary 1.85 and Proposition 1.90, pp.32--33: conjugation stability before the smooth-ambient normality test.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-ambient-normality-geometric] with $k=F$, $J=G$ and $N=U$, choosing $F$ itself as algebraic closure. The ambient group $G$ is smooth and affine of finite type, $U$ is a closed affine finite-type subgroup by step 1, and step 2 establishes its scheme-theoretic stability under every $g\in G(F)$. The cited statement therefore gives normality of $U$ in $G$ on all commutative $F$-algebras, including nonreduced algebras.

source.place: Corollary 1.85, printed p.32 (the criterion used in Proposition 1.90, p.33).

proof.text: Now $U\subseteq G$ is smooth, connected, closed, normal and unipotent. The definition [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology] is stated after extension to an algebraic closure $\iota:F\to\overline F$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Since $F$ is algebraically closed, every element of $\overline F$ is a root of a polynomial over $\iota(F)$, which splits over $\iota(F)$; so $\iota$ is an isomorphism, and extension along it identifies $G_{\overline F},M_{\overline F},U_{\overline F}$ with $G,M,U$, preserving closed immersions, normality, smoothness, connectedness and the matrices of faithful representations. Reductivity of $G$ therefore forces $U=1$. For every smooth connected closed normal unipotent subgroup $W\subseteq M_{\overline F}\cong M$, the containment assertion of [lem-sfb-unipotent-radical-existence] gives $W\subseteq U=1$, so $W=1$. Together with the given smoothness, connectedness of $M_{\overline F}\cong M$ and the affine finite-type conclusion of step 1, this is exactly reductivity of $M$ in the same definition. For $M=1$ the argument gives $U=W=1$ as well.

source.place: Section 6.46, printed p.135: reductivity is triviality of the unipotent radical; Corollary 21.53, printed p.441, conclusion.

proof_origin.place: Alternative proof of Corollary 21.53 from Section 6.46 and Corollary 1.85: write out invariance of the largest unipotent normal subgroup under conjugation. This is a node-level argument, not a change to the unit route.
